catalog_quote: This process of vowel reduction is undoubtedly an effect of phonetic stress. In a protoform with two syllables, only the one receiving stress was preserved, while the unstressed vowel eventually disappeared (e.g., *mate > mat). ... In the case of northern Vanuatu languages, there is every likelihood that the final consonants of POc forms had been lost at some stage (e.g., 'ten' *saŋapuluq > *saŋapulu); this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *saŋapulu). ... The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language. [fn. 2, p. 443:] Data for Lehalurup come from Codrington (1885) and Tryon (1976). [Table 4, p. 476:] LHR Lehalurup | loss of posttonic V2? all | vowel hybridization? yes | primary vs. secondary stress outcome? same | pretonic vowel Vi: total assimilation

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Torres-Banks languages generally (the 17-language sample includes Lehalurup/Löyöp = LHR), word stress falls on the final syllable, the historical penult having become final after loss of posttonic vowels. This is an areal generalization ('essentially all the languages of the area'), not a Löyöp-specific description.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing synchronic; only the reconstructed pre-modern pattern (primary stress on the penult, secondary stress every second syllable leftward) is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'essentially all' languages of the area without naming exceptions (Mota, which kept many final vowels, is the likely reservation). For LHR specifically, fn. 2 p. 443 states the 2005 data came from Codrington (1885) and Tryon (1976), i.e. the author had not yet done his own Löyöp fieldwork (2006-2007 per the Pangloss archive).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, diachronically framed statement; no discussion of phrase-level prosody or citation forms for Löyöp. No later first-hand François publication (2011 JHL, 2012 IJSL, 2021 Pangloss notes) states Löyöp stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Löyöp [løjøp] (glottocode leha1244, ISO urr) = 'Lehalurup' of Tryon 1976 / François 2005 (code LHR; later LYP) = 'Rowa': speakers relocated from the Rowa (Reef) Islands to Divers' Bay, E. Ureparapara c. 1930 (Lynch & Crowley 2001:39; Pangloss). Distinct from Lehali (lehal1245.. i.e. Glottolog 'Lehali', ISO tql) on W/N Ureparapara. Codrington 1885's 'Norbarbar' sketch describes the pre-1930 'bay on the Eastern side' dialect plus Retan, so its identity with modern Löyöp is uncertain, although François 2005 used it as his LHR source. The quoted stress statement is areal (all Torres-Banks languages), not specific to Löyöp.
